FW OBIT - Turbulent Transition

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Interviews and reflections about the man who played a critical role in South Africa's turbulent transition into a democracy. Tracing back FW de Klerk's political career takes us through some of the most momentous historical periods of the country.

Summary:
A tapestry of South Africa's recent history, using national archive footage, old newspaper clippings, shots of historical documents, old
family photographs to lay over the interviews. These are interview with a close friend, political mentee, political opponent, historian and a journalist's reflection of the poignant times of de Klerk's career and by extension the country's history.

Further information:
The FW de Klerk Foundation has made itself available to tap into as a source for archive material and photographs. Parliament will supply some of his historical addresses made in the National Assembly, these are in DVD format but we'll organise that they be converted. North West University, Potchefstroom campus, his alma mater will share visuals of the campus as well old photographs they may have from when he was a student there and chancellor in the 90s. Archives relating to his presidency and the transition are kept at the University of Free State, the liberian at the FW de Klerk library has availed herself to do a 'guided tour' type interview. Once we know what archive material MNET has we'll be able to asses how we use and incorporate the visuals into the piece.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel budget to Free State university, this trip will also help us shoot GVs of relevant parts of Bloemfontein.
Cape Town crew for interview with Dave Steward.

Dr. Piet Croucamp
Mr. Dave Steward long time friend and spokesperson

Script:


VO UPSOUND VISUALS

LINK Union Buildings;

When FW de Klerk first arrived here as State President in 1989, the writing was on the wall: the apartheid regime - facing mounting international condemnation and feeling the impact of global sanctions - was growing increadingly brutal and opressive.

Something had to give.




Roelf Meyer was appointed Minister of Defence by De Klerk in 1991 , and later headed up the team that negotiated a settlement with the ANC.






















5:05 R –he was a person who concentrated on good relations. you can’t really describe him as him being a dominant person
5;54 R – ja eh if ew jump from there to what he actually became known for I think, pragmatism is a good description. He followed an ideological line, he was on the conservative side of the national party thinking, he was less reform orientated than some of the others who were in cabinet at that stage. He was trusted. And he had a mindset that was eh problem solving by orientation and I think that can be best described by a pragmatic approach.
Roelf walking into frame, sits on chair


NOTE - pic of roelf and de klerk
As a young politician, FW de Klerk’s career developed quickly. His father, Jan de Klerk, was a former senator, His uncle was J.G Strijdom, the South African prime minister in the 50s.
He was always surrounded by influential figures in the Afrikaans community, a quintessential nationalist.


De Klerk cut his teeth as the leader of the youth league of the National Party at Potchefstroom university, where he studied law. He soon became a member of parliament before serving in various ministerial positions.

Over the years de Klerk had been a loyal member of the regime, primed for higher office.






02:20 Dr – the instinct of the national party was that, since the 1970s, 60s and 80s, were only two; it was either fight or flight and I think that’s how they perceived politics. Er we either gonna win this war against liberation movements , against communism, against black south Africans or there’s no place for us in South Africa. .de klerk was different in a sense in that the fight or flight optionv was there but he was a pragmatist, There is no more money to fight, there is no more money to supply the war, there is no more money to supply the military machine to sustain the fight. that’s how his mind worked, 4:15 he wasn’t a militarized man CRROUCAMP walking into frame sitting down introducing himself

DR PIET CROUCAMP - SENIOR POLITICS LECTURER AT NORTH WEST UNIVERSITY
De Klerk’s predecessor was the combative PW Botha, who, at the height of tensions in 1985 had resisted reform and instead declared a state-of-emergency.



5 years later, the 2nd of February 1990, marked an unexpected shift in ideology. De Klerk, recently elected president, announced the imminent release of Nelson Mandela and other political prisoners, as well as the unbanning of the ANC and other liberation movements. Getty pictures of PW Botha
Roelf

15;36 within afrikaanerhood, within national party also, there were definitely certain segments would not have expected it to be so abrupt, so quick, so swiftly, without any notice and many would have been surprised by that. And also a lot of resistance. We can recall what the conservative party, terech and his group said about this announcement, they called it black Friday.



Dave Steward, an aide and lifelong friend to the former statesman, ran De Klerk’s foundation
Dave

1;08 on the right wing, FW de klerk is excoriated as a sell out, traitor to the Afrikaaner people most of the hate mail we receive is from the right wing.
DAVE13;00 – I think de klerk’s motivation was his sense that he had an opportunity as a leader to put write what was manifestly wrong. He realised that this could only be achieved only by negotiations with all south africa’s significant political parties and population groups including the ANC. He realised that this would mean the end of white national sovereignty.k.
And the push back from white conservatives was visceral.
it was in an atmosphere of fear, suspicion but also hope that the CODESA talks - aimed at a peaceful transition to democracy - began; former foes on opposite sides of the negotiating table.


The stakes were high:

In June, 1992, 45 people were killed in Boipatong, south of Jo’burg. It’s alleged the massacre, carried out by members of the IFP against ANC supporters, was orchestrated by the apartheid police. The implied involvement of the third force was not officially confirmed but was widely believed.

The images of dead bodies captured by Carte Blanche at the time were horrifying .

BOIPATONG CB INSERT




































Bantu Holomisa, now leader of the UDM, says the massacre almost collapsed the negotiations.

BANTU :
08:33 the Boipatong Massacre I remember , it happened when I was in Europe with Madiba , we came back and there was a big funeral , the ANC and its Allies decided to cut off the negotiations tensions were high //
Croump
there was a particular incentive in stirring this violence on and there’s no doubt about that from the National Party rogues.


//There was demand that this negotiation must be mediated by either the international community because De Klerk and his government are negotiating in bad faith.
09:48 De Klerk will never escape that accusation when his forces applied for amnesty during the TRC, they would say yes we were sanctioned by the government to do A,B and C.

Days after the massacre, President de Klerk visited the township. Chaos ensued between police and crowds.

83 year old Maseabatha Khunou recounts the moment she found her son’s body riddled by bullets, shot at allegedly by police .








07;03 – 07;13 how dare you ask me what happened, my child is dead, shoot me too, I die with my child.
08;28 he was shot on this side of his body. The left side, all the way down. Blood was coming out of his mouth and I wiped it away.
Her story wasn’t heard at the TRC nor was the incident ever investigated, Decades later there’s no closure and no justice for Khunou. And for many other families who suffered similar atrocities, like the CRADOCK 4, and activist NOKTHULA SIMELANE who was abducted by the special branch of the apartheid police 40 years ago, never to be seen again.

Through his political career, de klerk remained a loyal member of the national party and was president during the period when some of these horrors unfolded, these are brutalities that have become synonymous with his legacy.

LINK UNION BUILDINGS
Many of these perpetrators were never tried in a court of law for these atrocities, leaving many questions about how high up these instructions would have come from.

It’s also his longtime reluctance to acknowledge Apartheid as a crime against humanity thta has tainted his name, late into his life.

Link Union Buildings :
Branded a traitor by many Afrikaners, and seen as as the last leader of an illegitimate ,discredited regime by the black majority, one cannot deny the crucial role FW de Klerk played in paving the way to democracy in the country,but decades on South Africans still have cause to reflect on his complex legacy.


Bantu: 25:56 Any legacy we can talk about is that he read the signals of change, occasioned by the cold war ,to freeing the world , so for him he read the signals and came to the table . at least he was prepared to engage.
Roelf :
Croucamp:
